newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian judge orders release of cartel property.
newsitem.headline: Colombian judge orders release of cartel property.

text.p: A "faceless" judge who sentenced Colombia's biggest drug lords to lenient prison terms also ordered the release of property and assets linked to their criminal empire, judicial officials said on Wednesday.

The order releasing an unspecified amount of assets linked to Cali cartel kingpins Gilberto and Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela is certain to add to the storm of controversy in Washington over the prison sentences handed down last week.

A spokeswoman for Alfonso Valdivieso, Colombia's chief prosecutor, said the judge's order in Cali would be appealed. She said the order did not mean all confiscated properties belonging to the billionaire Rodriguez brothers would be returned to them, only those properties and assets that were in the hands of "third parties" when they were confiscated.
But local media called the ruling an outrage since many of the properties affected were in the hands of suspected "testaferros," known cartel frontmen, when they were seized.
Colombia has special tribunals of anonymous or faceless judges as a security measure to protect them from assassinations or intimidations by criminal elements.

The Rodriguezes were sentenced to 18 and 21 years in prison for crimes including drug trafficking and illegal weapons possession but their jail terms were halved under Colombia's elaborate plea-bargaining programme. The pair, who masterminded what U.S. officials have described as the world's biggest-ever drug trafficking organisation, could walk free in as little as five years with time off for good behaviour.

By contrast, a judge in the northwest city of Medellin sentenced a brother of the late drug lord Pablo Escobar to 26 years in prison on Wednesday for crimes including drug trafficking, kidnapping and theft.

Court officials said Roberto Escobar Gaviria, who was blinded and left partly deaf by a letter bomb that exploded in his jail cell in 1993, was eligible to have his sentence reduced by only about eight years. Under current law the maximum sentence for drug trafficking in Colombia is 24 years.

The handling of the Rodriguez case has drawn a sharp rebuke from U.S. drug czar Barry McCaffrey and other officials in Washington, which "decertified" Colombia last year as a full-fledged partner in the global anti-drug fight.

The Clinton administration must announce by March 1 whether Colombia will remain on a list of countries that have failed to participate actively enough in the drug fight. There are widespread fears in Colombia, especially since last week, that renewed decertification could trigger punitive commercial sanctions, which Washington did not choose to apply last year.

Addressing those fears in a speech on Wednesday during a visit to the impoverished, drug-infested southern province of Caqueta, President Ernesto Samper urged his countrymen to avoid falling into "a situation of collective hysteria ... over the subject of certification."
Samper, whose alleged ties to the Cali cartel were cited among the leading reasons for last year's decertification, said "no country has the right to certify another's conduct."
